# VulcanBench

> An open-source coding benchmark that measures frontier language models on real merged
> open-source pull requests, graded by deterministic hidden tests. Unusually for a coding
> benchmark, every model is swept across its whole reasoning-effort ladder (low, medium,
> high, xhigh, max) rather than measured only at maximum effort, and cost, wall-clock time,
> agent steps, and token use are reported alongside accuracy.

VulcanBench is run by Morgan Linton, Cofounder and CTO of Bold Metrics. Tasks come from pull
requests merged after the evaluated models' training cutoffs, so solutions cannot have been
memorised. Grading is done by hidden tests validated to fail on the base commit and pass on
the merged fix; no model judges another model. The harness and every eval are open source.

## Key pages
- [Leaderboard](https://vulcanbench.com/leaderboard.html): every model on the current v3 suite, ranked at every effort level, with pass@1, cost per task, and minutes per task.
- [Benchmarks](https://vulcanbench.com/benchmarks.html): the full published record of technical reports, newest first.
- [Methodology](https://vulcanbench.com/methodology.html): how tasks are selected, decontaminated, sandboxed, and graded.
- [Blog](https://vulcanbench.com/blog.html): writing about why VulcanBench exists and what the effort knob keeps showing.
- [Custom evals](https://vulcanbench.com/benchmark-your-stack.html): private eval suites built from a team's own repositories, returned as a model-routing policy.
- [Benchmark your model](https://vulcanbench.com/benchmark-your-model.html): for labs measuring their own model, fine-tune, or agent scaffold.

## Blog posts
- [Why I started VulcanBench, and my journey building evals and benchmarking models across effort levels](https://vulcanbench.com/blog/01-why-i-started-vulcanbench.html): Morgan Linton on the $300,000-a-year model bill that led him to build evals on his own team's codebase, the idea of a difficulty-aware multi-model execution layer, and why benchmarks measured only at Max effort gave him no usable signal. His team's bill fell to under $30,000/year.

## Recurring findings
- Higher reasoning effort frequently does not improve pass@1 on real engineering tasks, and on several models it reduces it while multiplying cost and wall-clock time.
- When accuracy converges between models, cost, token use, and time are the signals that separate them.
- The agent harness a model runs inside can be worth more points than the choice of model.
